title: Production DevOps, deployment strategies, and SRE
description: Blue-Green, Canary, Rolling deployments, expand-and-contract database migrations, Kubernetes health probes, and graceful shutdown.

questions.text: In a Canary Deployment, how is traffic routed to the newly deployed software version?

options.text: 100% of traffic is switched to the new environment instantaneously
A tiny percentage of live user traffic (e.g. 2% to 5%) is routed to the new version while monitoring error rates and latency before gradually ramping up to 100%
Only automated synthetic test bots are permitted to access the canary version
Traffic is alternated between version A and B based on odd and even seconds

questions.explanation: Canary deployments expose a small subset of real user traffic to the new release. Observability monitors P99 latency and error rates; if anomalies appear, traffic is rolled back with minimal user blast radius.

questions.text: How does the 'Expand and Contract' (Parallel Run) pattern achieve zero-downtime database schema migrations during rolling deployments?

options.text: By locking the database table for 10 minutes at midnight
Phase 1: Expand by adding new columns without deleting old ones; Phase 2: Deploy code writing to both; Phase 3: Contract by dropping old columns only after all old app versions are retired
By migrating the database to a NoSQL key-value store
By creating a brand new database cluster for each deployment

questions.explanation: Because rolling deployments have old and new app versions running concurrently, dropping or renaming a column in-place breaks old pods. Expand-and-contract ensures backwards and forwards compatibility across deployment phases.

questions.text: What is the critical distinction between a Kubernetes Liveness Probe and a Readiness Probe?

options.text: Liveness determines if the container is running (if it fails, Kubelet restarts it); Readiness determines if the container is ready to accept traffic (if it fails, Kubelet removes it from service endpoints)
Liveness is for HTTP; Readiness is for gRPC
Liveness runs only once at startup; Readiness runs continuously
There is no difference; they are interchangeable

questions.explanation: If a pod is overloaded or warming up its local cache, failing a Readiness probe cleanly removes it from load balancer routing without terminating it. Failing a Liveness probe kills and restarts the container, which can cause cascading crash loops if dependencies are down.

questions.text: When a containerized backend receives a SIGTERM signal during a rolling deployment, what should its Graceful Shutdown sequence do?

options.text: Stop accepting new incoming connections, finish processing in-flight active requests, close database connection pools and background workers, and then exit before SIGKILL arrives
Ignore the signal and continue running indefinitely
Flush all cache keys to disk synchronously

questions.explanation: A graceful shutdown prevents dropping client connections in-flight: the process unregisters from service discovery, stops accepting new requests, drains active HTTP requests within the termination grace period (e.g. 30s), closes DB pools, and cleanly exits.

questions.text: In a Blue-Green deployment, both environments (Blue = current live, Green = new version) run simultaneously, allowing instantaneous rollback by switching the router/load balancer back to Blue.
questions.explanation: True. Blue-Green maintains two identical production environments. The new code is tested on Green in isolation; flipping the router switches 100% of user traffic to Green. If an issue is detected, switching back to Blue takes seconds.
